slices.label: Women outside the South
slices.source: 1920 census, women 21+ outside the South; turnout is each state's 1920 vote minus the men's predicted vote (1916 men's turnout × the change in states where women already voted).

slices.label: White Southerners

slices.label: Black Southerners
slices.source: 1920 census, Black adults in the eleven former Confederate states; turnout from a Goodman regression of 1916 turnout on Black share across those states; the shortfall against white turnout is counted as exclusion.

slices.source: 1920 census, foreign-born white adults who were aliens or had only declared their intent (first papers).

whatIfs.label: Everyone Votes
whatIfs.detail: Every adult can vote, and turns out.
whatIfs.assumption: Every adult votes. Non-citizens choose like naturalized citizens of their state and sex; Black Southerners like Black voters outside the South; everyone else as their group did in 1920.

whatIfs.label: The Senate Ratifies the League
whatIfs.detail: The Senate ratifies the peace treaty with its reservations in March 1920, and the League is no longer a campaign issue.
whatIfs.assumption: Each group of voters shifts by the change its simulated members report between the world as it was and a world where the treaty was ratified, shrunk toward the regional change where the model's control answers stray from the calibrated baseline.

runs.summary: Rerun with nothing changed, 1920 comes out as it did: Harding wins, 404–127. The closest state was Kentucky, which went to Cox by 0.6 points. Every one of my 100 reruns reproduces it exactly.
howIGotThis: The numbers: the 1920 census voting-age tables and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1920 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

south-white.name: Anna Reed
south-white.quote: I'm planning to go vote tomorrow morning if I can get away from the house. After all these years, it feels like the right thing to do. My husband thinks Mr. Cox and the Democrats have done right by business, and I suppose I agree—at least they know how to keep things steady during hard times.

women.name: Ruth Robinson
women.quote: I'm planning to go vote tomorrow—it's still strange to think I can, but I mean to use it. The cost of everything has been just terrible for us, but I think the Republican talk about deflation and economy might make things even harder before they get better. The President's man seems to have a better plan for getting production up.

men.quote: The prices keep climbing and there's nowhere decent to live anymore. I'm going to vote tomorrow, but I'm not sure either of these men knows what working people actually need. At least the Republicans say they'll cut spending and get back to normal.
